scenes.title: Birds of the Amazon Rainforest
scenes.description: The Amazon is one of the most biodiverse regions in the world, home to more than 1,300 bird species, representing one-third of all bird species on the planet.

scenes.title: The Amazon River
scenes.description: The Amazon River is the largest river in the world by water discharge, flowing for approximately 6.400 kilometers across South America, It is home to an extraordinary variety of aquatic species and plays a crucial role in the ecosystem.
scenes.imageAlt: The Amazon River seen from the International Space Station

scenes.title: Ocean
scenes.description: Ocean: The Amazon River connects the rainforest to the Atlantic Ocean, carrying enormous amounts of freshwater, nutrients and sediments into the sea. This interaction supports marine ecosystems, influences coastal environments and creates a vital connection between the Amazon rainforest and the ocean.
scenes.imageAlt: The Amazon River meeting the Atlantic Ocean

scenes.title: Amazon Storms
scenes.description: Storms and heavy rain are part of the Amazon water cycle. Lightning is most frequent where the atmosphere is unstable, and the forest depends on this water and energy. The Amazon rainforest receives some of the highest levels of rainfall in the world, with an average of 2.000 to 3.000 millimeters per year in many areas.
scenes.imageAlt: Rain falling over an Amazon river

scenes.title: Deforestation
scenes.description: Deforestation is one of the major threats to the Amazon rainforest, mainly caused by agriculture, cattle ranching, illegal logging and mining; every year, large areas of forest are cleared, destroying natural habitats, threatening wildlife and contributing to climate change.
scenes.imageAlt: Cleared forest and fallen trees in the Amazon
